title: Hormone Receptor-Positive HER2-Negative Oligometastatic Breast Cancer: prognostic stratification and pattern of progression.
abstract: Background The management of oligometastatic breast cancer (OMBC) remains controversial, particularly regarding selection for local ablative treatment (LAT). In HR+/HER2- OMBC, where prolonged survival is often the case, improved stratification and characterization of progression may guide treatment. We aimed to define prognostic subsets, assess the contribution of Modern-Imaging-Methods (MIMs; 18F-FDG-PET/CT or WB-MRI) to LAT selection, and describe progression after first-line therapy in these subgroups of patients. Materials and methods All consecutive patients with HR+/HER2- OMBC treated at our institution between 2012 and 2020 were included. OMBC was defined as ≤ 5 metastases. Prognostic factors including biological subtype, anatomical distribution, imaging modality, and LAT were evaluated for overall and progression-free survival (OS, PFS). Results Among 145 patients (median follow-up 82.8 months), median OS and PFS were, respectively, 81.1 and 26.5 months. Luminal-A-like subtypes, absence of liver metastases, and use of MIMs independently predicted better survival. LAT improved PFS (hazard ratio [HR]=0.52; 95%CI[0.29-0.91], p=0.0233) and showed a trend toward longer OS. In patients staged with MIMs, LAT significantly improved both OS (HR = 0.29; 95%CI[0.12-0.73], p=0.008) and PFS (HR = 0.40; 95%CI[0.21-0.77], p=0.0064). After first-line systemic therapy, only 18% developed polymetastatic progression. Conclusion In HR+/HER2- OMBC, three actionable considerations emerge: staging must incorporate modern imaging to accurately define metastatic burden; LAT may be considered in selected patients with low-grade disease, absence of liver metastases, and long disease-free interval; in oligoprogression after first-line therapy, LAT should be re-evaluated within a multidisciplinary setting. These data offer pragmatic benchmarks to individualize treatment while awaiting definitive randomized evidence.

title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Tumor-Derived DNA Analysis Aids in the Diagnosis of Postpartum Diffuse Midline Glioma.
abstract: Background Gliomas diagnosed during pregnancy or postpartum pose diagnostic and management challenges. Neurologic symptoms may be attributed to physiological changes of pregnancy or the postpartum state, possibly delaying evaluation. When lesions arise in high-risk locations, such as the brainstem, tissue biopsy is frequently infeasible, further complicating the diagnostic process. Patient presentation A 28-year-old woman developed dysphagia during pregnancy, which persisted and gradually worsened after delivery. Postpartum evaluation identified a right thyroid nodule, subsequently diagnosed as papillary thyroid carcinoma following hemithyroidectomy. Eight months postpartum, the patient experienced progressive dysphagia, headaches, and dizziness. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an expansile medullary lesion concerning for a high-grade primary brainstem tumor. Due to the brainstem location, biopsy was infeasible, and empiric chemoradiation was initiated for presumed high-grade glioma. Molecular findings Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tumor-derived nucleic acid analysis using Summit™ 2.0 identified an H3-3A K28M alteration, along with co-occurring pathogenic alterations in NF1 and TP53. In conjunction with the clinical and radiographic findings, these molecular results supported classification of the tumor as diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered. Management and outcome Following completion of chemoradiation, dordaviprone therapy was initiated. At the most recent documented follow-up in January 2026, brain MRI demonstrated decreased size and enhancement of the medullary lesion, accompanied by improvement in dysphagia, headaches, dystonic movements, balance, and overall performance status. Conclusions This case demonstrates that cerebrospinal fluid-based genomic profiling can provide clinically meaningful molecular information when tissue diagnosis is contraindicated and can inform treatment planning for patients with anatomically inaccessible central nervous system tumors. It also highlights the significance of ongoing evaluation of persistent neurologic symptoms during pregnancy and the postpartum period.

title: Pelvic Insufficiency Fractures After Chemoradiotherapy for Cervical Cancer: Incidence, Long-Term Outcomes, and Survivorship Management.
abstract: Pelvic insufficiency fractures, a late complication of chemoradiotherapy for cervical cancer, can cause pain and functional impairment. Although most studies have reported incidence rates and risk factors, few have examined clinical presentation, long-term symptom burden, or the impact on survivorship. We conducted a retrospective study of patients with cervical cancer treated with chemoradiotherapy from 2018 to 2024. We extracted clinical characteristics, treatment details, dosimetric parameters, imaging studies documenting pelvic insufficiency fractures, and clinical outcomes from the electronic medical record. We used the Kaplan-Meier method to estimate the probability of pelvic insufficiency fractures and univariate Cox regression to assess clinical and dosimetric factors associated with their development. The cohort comprised 153 patients (median follow-up: 41.4 months). After chemoradiotherapy, 18 patients (11.8%) developed radiologically confirmed pelvic insufficiency fractures (median time to diagnosis: 9.5 months; probability of pelvic insufficiency fracture at 24 months: 11.4%). PET-CT and/or MRI showed that most pelvic insufficiency fractures involved the sacrum. No statistically significant clinical or dosimetric predictors of pelvic insufficiency fractures were identified. All symptomatic patients (n = 15, 83%) required referral to pain-management services (median observed duration of symptoms: 37 months). No symptomatic patient achieved documented complete symptom resolution during the available follow-up. Most pelvic insufficiency fractures presented with new-onset pelvic or sacral pain within two years of completing chemoradiotherapy. The lack of clinical or dosimetric predictors suggests a multifactorial etiology of fracture risk. Persistent pain, despite multimodal supportive care, led to long-term morbidity. These findings underscore the need for prospective studies to develop evidence-based preventive strategies, survivorship assessments, and management pathways.

title: Cardiovascular risk stratification using chest CT in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the diagnostic and prognostic value of incidentally detected coronary artery calcification (CAC) on routine chest computed tomography (CT) for cardiovascular risk stratification in patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM). Methods In this single-centre cross-sectional study, adult patients with IIM who underwent noncardiac, nongated high-resolution chest CT (HRCT) were included. CAC was visually categorized as absent, mild, moderate, or severe. Diagnostic performance for established coronary artery disease (CAD) and established cardiovascular (CV) events was assessed. Kaplan-Meier analyses evaluated CV death-free survival, and multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with CAC. A matched systemic sclerosis (SSc) cohort served as validation cohort. Results Among 234 patients with IIM (mean age 57.1±15.9 years; 70.1% female), CAC was present in 43.2%. Higher CAC thresholds showed greater specificity for established CAD and prior CV events, whereas lower thresholds were more sensitive. CAC was associated with reduced CV death-free survival (log-rank p = 0.0095), with a stepwise decline across CAC severity categories. Findings were similar in the matched SSc cohort. Increasing CAC burden was associated with older age, smoking, higher CV risk burden, interstitial lung disease, and higher disease activity. In adjusted analyses, high disease activity was independently associated with moderate CAC (OR 4.01, 95% CI 1.29-12.50), while a higher number of concomitant DMARDs was associated with severe CAC (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.27-5.11). Conclusion Incidentally detected CAC on routine chest CT provides diagnostic and prognostic information in IIM and may represent a pragmatic approach to improve cardiovascular risk stratification in this high-risk population.

title: The Efficacy of Erector Spinae Plane Block Versus Subcostal Transversus Abdominis Plane Block in Laparoscopic Nephrectomy: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Objectives This study compared the efficacy and safety of erector spinae plane block (ESPB) versus subcostal transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block in reducing postoperative pain among patients undergoing laparoscopic nephrectomy. Methods This randomized clinical trial enrolled 70 adult patients, ASA physical status I or II, who underwent total (radical) laparoscopic nephrectomy under general anesthesia. Patients were randomly assigned to 2 groups. Group ESPB received an ultrasound-guided ESPB at the T7 transverse process level, while group TAP received an ultrasound-guided subcostal TAP block. The primary outcome was the total amount of morphine consumed at 6 and 24 hours postoperatively. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of patients requiring opioid analgesia, time to rescue analgesia, visual analog scale of pain intensity, time to postoperative ambulation, intraoperative and postoperative hemodynamics, arterial partial pressure of oxygen to fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO 2 /FiO 2 or P /F) ratio, and incidence of complications. Results Compared with the TAP group, the ESPB group exhibited significantly lower median morphine consumption at 24 hours ( P =0.032), prolonged time to first analgesic rescue ( P =0.049), and lower incidence of rescue morphine requirement (OR=0.23; 95% CI=0.06-0.94; P =0.031), with lower visual analog scale pain scores at 12, 18, and 24 hours postoperatively ( P <0.001). The mean arterial blood pressure and heart rates were comparable between groups. No significant adverse effects from either approach. Discussion In laparoscopic nephrectomy, ultrasound-guided ESPB may safely and effectively be used to improve pain management and reduce pain intensity, with stable hemodynamics and a comparable risk of postoperative complications to the ultrasound-guided subcostal TAP block.

title: Neonatal Cardiac Tamponade Related to Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter: A Rare Case Report.
abstract: Background Peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) are commonly used in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) to provide prolonged intravenous access for preterm and critically ill infants. They are generally preferred over surgically placed central venous catheters because of easier insertion and, in some settings, lower infection rates. However, rare but life-threatening complications may occur. Cardiac tamponade, resulting from catheter malposition or delayed migration with perforation of the superior vena cava (SVC) or cardiac wall, is one such complication. This case highlights the need for vigilant monitoring even when initial catheter placement is confirmed as correct. Clinical findings A male infant born at 32 weeks' gestation with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) required mechanical ventilation and surfactant therapy. A PICC was inserted through the right radial vein, and radiographic assessment confirmed appropriate positioning in the SVC. The infant initially improved. On day 10 of NICU admission, he developed sudden respiratory distress, hypotonia, bradycardia, and cardiovascular collapse. Diagnosis Echocardiography demonstrated severe pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade due to SVC perforation by the PICC tip. Intervention and outcome The catheter was immediately removed, and emergency pericardiocentesis was performed. Despite aggressive resuscitation, the infant died on day 11 of life. Practice recommendations Delayed perforation can occur days after apparently correct placement. Preventive strategies should include risk-stratified catheter positioning, preference for lower SVC tip placement, routine echocardiographic surveillance especially after the first week and enhanced staff training for early recognition of warning signs. Continuous quality improvement and readiness for emergency intervention are essential to improve neonatal outcomes.

title: Feasibility of opportunistic osteoporosis screening using ankle CT Hounsfield units in older adults with ankle fractures.
abstract: Background Fragility fractures reveal osteoporosis, but ankle fractures are not consistently defined as fragility fractures. CT-derived Hounsfield unit measurements may provide an opportunistic method to identify patients at risk for osteoporosis. Purpose This study investigated the relationship between Hounsfield units (HU) from ankle CT scans and bone mineral density (BMD) measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA), with the aim of determining whether sufficient signal exists between ankle HU and DEXA-derived BMD to justify a larger prospective validation study, rather than to establish a definitive diagnostic tool. Study design/level of evidence Retrospective correlation study. Level III. Methods Patients aged 55 years or older, who underwent open reduction and internal fixation for OTA/AO 44 A-C ankle fractures between 2012 and 2024 and had both a preoperative ankle CT and a DEXA scan within 1 year of injury, were reviewed. HU values of the distal tibia and fibula were measured using standardized elliptical regions of interest. Multivariate linear regression was performed with the lowest DEXA T-score as the dependent variable, with HU values, and BMI as independent variables. Results A total of 57 patients (87.7% female, mean age 69.67 ± 9.24 years) were included. The average ankle HU was 192.43 ± 60.04, and the mean T-score was -1.73 ± 0.96. Regression analysis demonstrated that HU values (B = 0.005, P = .021) and BMI (B = 0.064, P = .007) were positively correlated with the T-score.The regression model was lowest T-score = 0.005*Ankle HU + 0.064*BMI-4.422.Based on this equation, an HU measurement of 106.64 or less, assuming a BMI of 21.7, correlated with osteoporosis. Conclusions Ankle HU values from CT scans demonstrated a positive association with DEXA-derived BMD, supporting proof-of-concept for ankle HU as a preliminary screening tool and providing methodological groundwork for future prospective validation. Given the high prevalence of osteopenia or osteoporosis in this population, ankle fractures should prompt formal bone health evaluation.

Patients aged 55 years or older, who underwent open reduction and internal fixation for OTA/AO 44 A-C ankle fractures between 2012 and 2024 and had both a preoperative ankle CT and a DEXA scan within 1 year of injury, were reviewed. HU values of the distal tibia and fibula were measured using standardized elliptical regions of interest. Multivariate linear regression was performed with the lowest DEXA T-score as the dependent variable, with HU values, and BMI as independent variables.

Results

A total of 57 patients (87.7% female, mean age 69.67 ± 9.24 years) were included. The average ankle HU was 192.43 ± 60.04, and the mean T-score was -1.73 ± 0.96. Regression analysis demonstrated that HU values (B = 0.005, P = .021) and BMI (B = 0.064, P = .007) were positively correlated with the T-score.The regression model was lowest T-score = 0.005*Ankle HU + 0.064*BMI-4.422.Based on this equation, an HU measurement of 106.64 or less, assuming a BMI of 21.7, correlated with osteoporosis.

Conclusions

Ankle HU values from CT scans demonstrated a positive association with DEXA-derived BMD, supporting proof-of-concept for ankle HU as a preliminary screening tool and providing methodological groundwork for future prospective validation. Given the high prevalence of osteopenia or osteoporosis in this population, ankle fractures should prompt formal bone health evaluation.

title: What is the Rate of Occult Vessel Abnormalities in High-Energy Tibial Plateau Fractures (OTA/AO 41)?
abstract: Objectives The aim of this study was to determine the rate of occult vascular abnormalities in high-energy tibial plateau fractures using computed tomography angiography (CTA). Methods . Design Prospective Cohort Study. Setting Single Academic Level I Trauma Center. Patient selection criteria Adult patients with a tibial plateau (OTA/AO 41) fracture, without clinical indication for CTA, that underwent knee-spanning external fixation were prospectively enrolled. Outcome measures and comparisons After external fixation, patients underwent CTA to evaluate fracture morphology and the vascular tree. Fisher exact test was used to determine correlations between arterial abnormalities and wound complications in patients with ≥90 days of follow-up. Results A total of 26 patients with 27 high-energy tibial plateau fractures were enrolled. Patients were predominantly male (n = 16, 61.5%) with a mean age of 45.1 ± 13.3 years. All patients had a blunt injury mechanism resulting in mostly closed (n = 25, 92.6%), bicondylar (n = 22, 81.5%) tibial plateau fractures. CTA demonstrated nonatherosclerosis vascular abnormalities in 3 patients (11.5%). Two had disrupted flow in the popliteal artery, and 1 had disrupted flow in the anterior tibial artery. No patient required vascular intervention. Atherosclerosis was appreciated in 6 (26.9%) patients. One of 3 patients (33%) with nonatherosclerosis vascular abnormalities had wound complications. Four of 24 patients (16.7%) without nonatherosclerosis vascular abnormalities had wound complications. There was no significant correlation between nonatherosclerosis vascular abnormalities and wound complications (abnormality present: 33.3% wound complication rate vs. no abnormality: 16.7%, P = 0.47). Conclusions Non atherosclerotic vascular abnormalities on CTA were found in approximately a 10th of high-energy tibial plateau fractures. In this cohort, vascular abnormalities were not associated with wound complications. CTA is likely not necessary in patients with tibial plateau fracture without clinical indications for CTA. Level of evidence Prognostic Level IV. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Outcomes Following Early Weight Bearing in Syndesmotic Injuries: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Objectives To compare outcomes of early weight bearing (EWB) at 2-weeks versus delayed weight bearing (DWB) at 6-weeks following operative ankle fracture fixation with syndesmotic stabilization. Methods Design: Prospective randomized controlled clinical trial. Setting Single Level 1 Trauma Center. Patient selection criteria Adult patients with operative rotational ankle fractures (OTA/AO 44A-C) and an intraoperative finding of syndesmotic injury following fracture fixation between September 2019 and September 2022 were included. All underwent dynamic syndesmotic stabilization utilizing a single suture button. Exclusion criteria were fibular fractures not amenable to length-stable fixation (e.g., Maisonneuve injuries), neuropathic diabetes, body weight ≥147.4 kg (325 lbs), imprisonment, pregnancy, lactation, end-stage renal disease, cognitive dysfunction, or polytrauma. Outcome measures and comparisons Maintenance of syndesmotic reduction at 1 year comparing immediate postoperative and 1-year CT scans of both ankles was the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes: pain (VAS), surgical satisfaction (SSQ-8), functional scores (AAOS Foot and Ankle), ankle range of motion, and complications. Results 106 patients were enrolled: 40 underwent syndesmotic fixation and were randomized. 16 patients (mean age 41 (21-80), 9 female, 7 male) randomized to EWB and 23 (mean age 43 (23-85), 12 female, 11 male) to DWB completed the study. Fracture types included lateral malleolar (OTA/AO 44A), bimalleolar and bimalleolar equivalent (OTA/AO 44B), and trimalleolar (OTA/AO 44C) fractures, with similar distribution between groups (p=0.96). EWB group had significantly higher pain scores (4.6 ± 2.8 vs 2.8 ± 2.3, p = 0.039) at the 2-week visit compared to DWB. At 1 year, dorsiflexion in the EWB group was significantly higher (14.2° ± 3.9° vs 7.7° ± 4.4°) than the DWB (p = 0.017). No significant difference in syndesmotic malreduction (p>0.99), loss of reduction (p>0.89), PROs, development of arthritis (p>1.0) or complication rates (p>0.37) at any other timepoint. Conclusions Early weight bearing at 2-weeks was noninferior to delayed weight bearing at 6-weeks following rotational ankle fracture fixation with a syndesmotic injury stabilized with flexible fixation. Level of evidence Level I.

title: Is the use of Porous Threaded Titanium Implants Associated with Lower Rates of Implant Migration in Elderly Pelvic Ring Injuries?
abstract: Objectives To determine if porous threaded titanium implant (PTTI) screws placed in the posterior pelvic ring as iliosacral (IS) or transiliac-transsacral (transsacral) were associated with implant positional changes, alterations in postoperative weightbearing restrictions, or the necessity of revision surgery in operatively managed geriatric pelvic ring injuries, compared to standard stainless steel screws. Methods Design Retrospective cohort study. Setting Academic Level I trauma center. Patient selection criteria Patients with operatively managed pelvic ring injuries (AO/OTA61) from January 2017 to June 2025, aged ≥65 years with a minimum of 6-months of radiographic and clinical follow-up were included.Outcome Measures and Comparisons: The primary study outcome was the incidence of postoperative pelvic ring implant positional changes, ≥2mm from immediate postoperative radiographs compared among patients treated with PTTI versus standard stainless steel screws for IS and transsacral fixation. Secondary outcomes included subsequent revision surgery or alterations in postoperative weightbearing restrictions related to implant positional changes. A multivariable logistic regression was used to determine associations of demographic, injury, and treatment variables with implant positional changes, the necessity for revision surgery, or negative changes in postoperative weightbearing restrictions. Results 271 patients were included; 215 (79.3%) were managed with standard screws, while PTTIs were used in 56 (20.7%). The standard screw cohort had a median follow-up of 8.9 months (interquartile range 6.2-11.3 months), while the PTTI cohort had a median follow-up of 9.1 months (interquartile range 6.3-10.9 months). Compared with the standard screw cohort, the PTTI cohort had a higher proportion of female sex (57.2% versus 73.2%, respectively; p=0.029) and a higher average age (74.0 years versus 78.6 years, respectively; p<0.001).Radiographic migration ≥2mm for posterior implants was observed in 18.1% of patients in the standard implant cohort versus 0.0% in the PTTI cohort (p<0.001). Implant migration >1cm was observed in 3.7% of patients in the standard implant cohort versus 0.0% in the PTTI group (p=0.231). The implant positional changes resulted in negative weightbearing restriction changes in 9 of 215 (4.2%) patients in the standard implant cohort compared with 0 of 56 in the PTTI cohort (p=0.120). Of the patients with standard implants, 9 (4.2%) underwent revision for posterior implant loosening, compared with 0 (0.0%) in the PTTI cohort.On multivariate analysis, posterior implant positional changes were associated with a protective effect from PTTI and anterior ring fixation (OR 0.1, 95% CI 0.0-0.7, p=0.023 and OR 0.2, 95% CI 0.1-0.4, p<0.001, respectively). The necessity for revision surgery or negative change in postoperative weightbearing restrictions was not significantly associated with PTTI use (OR 0.3, 95% CI 0.1-1.3, p=0.106). Conclusions In geriatric pelvic ring injuries, PTTIs had no migration after placement and were associated with a lower incidence of any implant positional change and posterior implant positional changes. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III.

title: Preoperative ultrasound in pediatric supracondylar fracture-related nerve injuries: intraoperative correlation in a tertiary referral retrospective case series.
abstract: Nerve palsy is a recognized complication of paediatric supracondylar humeral fractures. Most injuries recover spontaneously, a subset require surgical exploration, and identifying those who may benefit from intervention remains challenging. High-resolution ultrasound has emerged as a potential adjunct for assessing nerve injury, although its utility in this setting remains incompletely defined. A retrospective case series was conducted at a tertiary peripheral nerve injury center. Children less than 16 years with persistent supracondylar fracture-related nerve palsy who underwent preoperative ultrasound and surgical exploration between 2018 and 2024 were included. Ultrasound findings were categorized as structural abnormality, compression/tethering, neuroma/swelling, or entrapment and were compared with intraoperative findings. Analysis was descriptive, focusing on ultrasound detection of nerve abnormality and concordance with surgical findings. Twenty-two patients were included (mean age: 7 years). All had surgically confirmed nerve pathology. Ultrasound demonstrated nerve abnormality in 21 out of 22 cases (95%). Compression/tethering was the most common finding (18/22), followed by structural abnormality (14/22), neuroma/swelling (7/22), and entrapment (2/22). Intraoperatively, structural abnormalities were identified in 17 cases, compression/tethering in 21, neuroma in 3, and entrapment in 4. Ultrasound frequently identified nerve abnormality but demonstrated variable concordance with intraoperative findings, including overestimation of neuroma (7 vs. 3 cases) and under-detection of entrapment (2 vs. 4 cases). Preoperative ultrasound frequently demonstrated abnormal nerve features in children with persistent palsy following supracondylar humeral fracture. However, its limited concordance in characterizing specific pathology restricts its role as a standalone decision-making tool. Ultrasound findings should be interpreted alongside clinical assessment when considering surgical exploration.

title: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium in adolescent athletes with acute groin pain: clinical and MRI features of a radiograph-occult injury pattern.
abstract: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium is an uncommon MRI finding in young athletes with acute groin pain and is frequently occult on plain radiographs. This study aimed to characterize its clinical presentation, MRI findings, associated injuries, and return-to-sport outcomes. This retrospective single-center case series included athletes aged ≤22 years who underwent MRI for acute sports-related groin pain with negative or inconclusive radiographs between 2017 and 2025. Patients meeting predefined MRI criteria for subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium were identified, and clinical, imaging, and outcome data were analyzed descriptively. Twenty of 91 patients (22.0%) met the MRI criteria. Their mean age was 13.9 ± 1.5 years, 19 (95%) were male, and 18 (90%) had open physes. Periosteal elevation was present in all patients, and 19 (95%) demonstrated a predominantly subperiosteal fluid collection, most commonly with a lentiform configuration. Associated anterior inferior iliac spine avulsion injury or intramuscular iliacus injury was identified in 10 patients (50%). All patients were managed nonoperatively and returned to unrestricted sports participation after progressive rehabilitation at a mean of 4.5 ± 2.2 weeks. Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium is a reproducible MRI finding in predominantly skeletally immature athletes with acute sports-related groin pain and negative or inconclusive radiographs. Recognition of periosteal elevation with a predominantly subperiosteal fluid collection may facilitate diagnosis of this radiograph-occult injury pattern. Although the underlying injury mechanism remains hypothetical, prospective studies are needed to clarify its clinical significance.

title: Open Reduction for Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip in the Newborn Hip Screening Era: Changing Patient Characteristics and Surgical Strategies Without Compromising Outcomes.
abstract: Introduction Newborn hip ultrasound scan (USS) for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) has significantly reduced the number of delayed cases. However, open reduction (OR) is still required when nonsurgical treatment fails in properly screened patients, as well as in neglected and late-presenting cases. The aim of this study is to compare the clinical and radiologic outcomes of OR for DDH between screened and neglected cases. Methods Patients diagnosed with DDH and who underwent OR at a single center were included and categorized into 2 groups: Screened patients with an unsuccessful nonoperative treatment attempt (group 1), and neglected patients due to misdiagnosis or lack of USS (group 2). Comparisons were performed between groups for demographic parameters, surgical characteristics, pre- and postoperative radiographic analyses, radiologic and clinical outcome assessments, and complications. Results One hundred thirteen patients (148 hips) were included (group 1=66 and group 2=82). Group 1 had younger median age at the time of OR (11 vs. 23.2 mo, P<0.001), less IHDI grade 3-4 ratio (74% vs. 90%, P<0.001) higher medial/anterior OR ratio (55% vs. 15%, P<0.001), lower rate of concomitant femoral (35% vs. 71%, P<0.001) and pelvic osteotomy (38% vs. 78%, P<0.001) as compared with group 2. PFGD (proximal femur growth disturbance) rates were similar between the 2 groups. No difference noted for Severin grade (good to excellent result 89% vs. 92%, P=0.42), McKay (excellent result 83% vs. 77%, P=0.21), revision (9.8% vs. 6.4%, P=0.33), reoperation for implant removal (14 vs. 20, P=0.23), and for pelvic osteotomy due to residual acetabular dysplasia (6 vs. 5, P=0.58). Conclusion Early detection of DDH through USS not only reduced delayed presentations but also altered the demographic, clinical, and surgical characteristics of patients requiring OR. Despite failed initial conservative management, screened patients achieved comparable radiologic and clinical outcomes to those of unscreened patients, with similar rates of complications and residual acetabular dysplasia. These findings suggest that newborn hip USS enables less extensive surgical management without compromising outcomes. Level of evidence Level III-retrospective comparative study.

title: Development of Screening Criteria to Detect Transthyretin Amyloid in the Ligamentum Flavum: Early Detection of Amyloidosis.
abstract: Study design Prospective cross-sectional study. Objective To develop and apply screening criteria for patients at risk of systemic amyloidosis undergoing routine lumbar decompression, using histopathological evaluation of ligamentum flavum (LF) tissue. Summary of background data Amyloidosis is the extracellular deposition of insoluble, misfolded proteins, leading to progressive multiorgan dysfunction. Although recent therapies can slow disease progression, they do not reverse existing organ damage, underscoring the importance of early detection. Musculoskeletal manifestations of amyloidosis, such as lumbar stenosis (LS), can precede cardiac symptoms, providing an opportunity for early detection and treatment. Amyloid deposition within the LF has been identified as a contributing factor to LF hypertrophy and spinal stenosis, yet no standardized guidelines exist for determining which patients should undergo LF tissue sampling during lumbar decompression surgery. Methods Patients with conditions linked to amyloidosis and axial T2 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) LF thickness >4.9 mm were prospectively enrolled. LF tissue samples were stained with Congo red (CR), and positive cases were subtyped. Patients with confirmed amyloid were referred for cardiac evaluation. Results Fifty patients were enrolled in the study; 14 (28%) had positive CR staining, and 10 (20%) were determined to have transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) (95% CI, 17.5-41.7% and 11.2-33.0%, respectively). LF was thicker in the positive cohort (6.3±0.6 vs. 5.6±0.8; P≤.001). There was no difference in age or number of levels decompressed. Six of the 14 patients elected to undergo further cardiac evaluation, including a 99mTc-PYP scan; all results were negative. Conclusion The screening criteria identified patients at risk for amyloidosis. 20% of patients were found to have ATTR, and those who completed cardiac evaluation had no evidence of cardiac involvement at the time of evaluation. While larger studies are needed, LF analysis during routine decompression may provide a practical method for early detection.

Patients with conditions linked to amyloidosis and axial T2 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) LF thickness >4.9 mm were prospectively enrolled. LF tissue samples were stained with Congo red (CR), and positive cases were subtyped. Patients with confirmed amyloid were referred for cardiac evaluation.

Results

Fifty patients were enrolled in the study; 14 (28%) had positive CR staining, and 10 (20%) were determined to have transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) (95% CI, 17.5-41.7% and 11.2-33.0%, respectively). LF was thicker in the positive cohort (6.3±0.6 vs. 5.6±0.8; P≤.001). There was no difference in age or number of levels decompressed. Six of the 14 patients elected to undergo further cardiac evaluation, including a 99mTc-PYP scan; all results were negative.

Conclusion

The screening criteria identified patients at risk for amyloidosis. 20% of patients were found to have ATTR, and those who completed cardiac evaluation had no evidence of cardiac involvement at the time of evaluation. While larger studies are needed, LF analysis during routine decompression may provide a practical method for early detection.

title: Development of a Multivariable Prognostic Model for Risk Stratification in C1 Fractures.
abstract: Study design Retrospective analysis of adult patients with radiographically confirmed C1 fractures treated across a single healthcare system including multiple level 1 trauma centers and multiple community hospitals (2015-22). The primary outcome was instability. Peri-operative outcomes and complications were also considered. Objective To evaluate radiographic and clinical predictors of instability or surgical management in patients with C1 fractures and to develop a multivariable prognostic model. Summary of background data Determining instability in C1 fractures remains challenging. Traditional criteria rely heavily on radiographic displacement thresholds, which may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of atlas fracture instability. Methods Demographic, clinical, and radiographic variables were analyzed including lateral mass displacement, dens fracture, neurologic deficit, age, sex, and body mass index. Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression was used to adjust for confounders and identify factors significantly associated with instability/operative treatment. Receiver operating characteristic analysis assessed model discrimination. A point-based instability risk score was derived from model coefficients. Results In adjusted analysis of Two hundred and seventy-nine patients, Lateral mass displacement (OR 1.20 per mm, 95% CI 1.09-1.33, P<0.001), dens fracture (OR 2.67, 95% CI 1.35-5.38, P=0.0047), and neurologic deficit (OR 5.22, 95% CI 1.69-16.1, P=0.0047) were significantly associated with instability or surgical management. The traditional 7-mm displacement threshold performed poorly (AUC 0.64, P=0.012). The multivariable model demonstrated good discrimination (AUC 0.75. Based on the final multivariable regression model, a point-based instability risk score was derived to estimate patient-specific risk with good predictive accuracy. Conclusions Instability in C1 fractures was significantly associated with several factors including increasing lateral mass displacement, dens fracture, and neurologic deficit. These parameters outperformed legacy assessment tools based on radiographic measurement. Our prognostic utility demonstrated improved predictive performance and may assist clinicians in risk stratification and treatment decision-making.

title: Anterior Lumbar Plexus Position on Preoperative Supine MRI Is Associated With Postoperative Motor Deficits After Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion at L4-5.
abstract: Study design Retrospective propensity score-matched case-control study. Objective To evaluate whether preoperative MRI-based psoas morphology, lumbar plexus position, iliac crest height, and psoas cross-sectional area (CSA) are associated with postoperative motor deficits (PMDs) following standalone lateral lumbar interbody fusion (SA-LLIF) at L4-L5. Summary of background data PMDs remain a recognized complication of LLIF. Although anatomical characteristics have been implicated in neurological risk, the clinical value of classifying these features on preoperative MRI remains incompletely understood. Methods Patients who developed PMDs after L4-L5 SA-LLIF were propensity score matched to patients without PMDs. Preoperative supine MRI was used to assess operative-side psoas morphology (Amaral classification), lumbar plexus position (Moro zones), iliac crest height, and absolute and height-adjusted psoas CSA. Conditional logistic regression analyses, including a multivariable model incorporating both psoas morphology and lumbar plexus position, were performed to evaluate their associations with PMDs. Results A total of 172 matched patients were included. An anterior lumbar plexus position extending beyond the midpoint of the vertebral body on preoperative supine MRI (Moro Zones 1-2) remained independently associated with PMDs after adjustment for psoas morphology (OR 14.37, 95% CI 1.78-115.95; P=0.012). Although Type III psoas morphology according to the Amaral classification was associated with increased odds of PMDs in univariable analysis (OR 4.77, 95% CI 1.65-13.76; P=0.004), this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for lumbar plexus position (OR 2.54, 95% CI 0.90-7.18; P=0.078). Iliac crest height, psoas CSA, and height-adjusted psoas CSA were not associated with PMDs. Conclusions Psoas morphology and lumbar plexus position on preoperative supine MRI were associated with PMDs following L4-L5 SA-LLIF. An anterior lumbar plexus position remained independently associated with PMDs after adjustment for psoas morphology. These findings support preoperative MRI-based anatomical assessment for neurological risk stratification and patient counseling.

title: Primary resistant disease is clinically heterogeneous in metastatic renal cell carcinoma treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab.
abstract: The study aimed to characterize clinical heterogeneity among patients with primary resistant disease (PRD) after first-line nivolumab plus ipilimumab (NIVO+IPI) for metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) and to explore clinical factors associated with death within 1 year among patients with PRD. We retrospectively analyzed 151 patients with mRCC who received first-line NIVO+IPI at four institutions in Japan between May 2018 and January 2025. PRD was defined as disease progression occurring within 3 months after treatment initiation, based on radiographic and clinical assessment, or death from any cause within the same period. For exploratory analyses, primary resistant disease with early mortality (PRD-EM) was defined as death within 1 year among patients with PRD. Survival was estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method. Because the PRD subgroup was small and several variables had sparse cell counts, associations with PRD-EM were assessed using Firth penalized logistic regression. PRD occurred in 31 of 151 patients (20.5%). Median overall survival was 3.9 months [95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.8-13.6] in patients with PRD and 46.7 months (95% CI = 38.8-62.8) in those without PRD (log-rank P < 0.001). Among patients with PRD, 20 of 31 (64.5%) met the exploratory PRD-EM definition. In the parsimonious two-variable Firth model, baseline C-reactive protein (CRP) ≥2 mg/dL [adjusted odds ratio (OR) = 7.95; 95% CI = 1.32-68.18; P = 0.023] and lymph node involvement (adjusted OR = 11.65; 95% CI = 1.78-142.82; P = 0.009) were associated with PRD-EM. PRD after first-line NIVO+IPI was associated with heterogeneous clinical outcomes. Elevated baseline CRP and lymph node involvement were associated with PRD-EM in an exploratory analysis. The PRD-EM classification and these associations require validation in larger independent cohorts before they can be used for clinical decision-making.

title: Diagnostic Performance of the Radiographic Assessment of Lung Edema Score for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome-Post Hoc Analysis of the "Validating Acute Lung Injury Biomarkers for Diagnosis" Study.
abstract: Objectives To determine the diagnostic accuracy of the Radiographic Assessment of Lung Edema (RALE) score for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and its interobserver reliability. Design Post hoc analysis of a prospective observational cohort study. Setting ICUs at Vanderbilt University Medical Center participating in the Validating Acute Lung Injury Biomarkers for Diagnosis study. Patients Adult patients receiving invasive ventilation for at least two consecutive days, with chest radiographs available on the first 2 ICU days. Interventions None. Measurements and main results Chest radiographs from the first 2 ICU days were scored independently by at least two experienced raters; scores were averaged per radiograph, and the highest averaged score from ICU day 1 or 2 was selected for analysis. The primary outcome was ARDS according to the Berlin definition during the first 2 ICU days. Of 236 patients, 92 (39%) had ARDS. The median RALE score was higher in patients with ARDS than in those without (29.5 [22.2-34.5] vs. 12.2 [7.5-17.8]; p < 0.01). The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.93 (95% CI, 0.90-0.96). At the optimal cutoff of 20, sensitivity was 85%, specificity 83%, positive predictive value 76%, and negative predictive value 90%. Interobserver reliability was high, with pairwise intraclass correlation coefficients ranging from 0.81 to 0.87. Conclusions In patients invasively ventilated for at least 2 days, the RALE score demonstrated excellent diagnostic accuracy for ARDS at a cutoff of 20, together with high interobserver reliability, supporting its potential role as a standardized radiographic tool in the diagnosis of ARDS.

title: Comprehensive role of fluorine-18-labeled fluorodeoxyglucose PET/computed tomography across the disease course of primary malignant melanoma of the esophagus.
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the clinical value of fluorine-18-labeled fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/computed tomography (CT) in managing primary malignant melanoma of the esophagus (PMME). Seventy patients with pathologically confirmed PMME between September 2011 and June 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. The diagnostic performance of 18F-FDG PET/CT was analyzed for evaluating primary tumors, lymph nodes, recurrence, metastasis, and its role in predicting treatment response. Among 20 patients who underwent preoperative evaluation, no significant differences in 18F-FDG uptake or tumor wall thickness were observed between T1 and T2/T3 tumors (all P > 0.05). Lesion-based analysis revealed that the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for lymph node evaluation was 0.923 for 18F-FDG PET/CT and 0.738 for contrast-enhanced CT, with sensitivities of 82.6 and 47.8%, and specificities of 98.0 and 97.0%, respectively. Among 25 patients who received nonsurgical treatment, significant differences were found in maximum standardized uptake value, metabolic tumor volume (MTV), total lesion glycolysis (TLG), and tumor wall thickness between responders and nonresponders (all P < 0.05). Multivariate analysis identified TLG as an independent predictor of treatment response (odds ratio = 0.950, P = 0.025). In 50 patients evaluated for distant metastases and postoperative recurrence, additional findings from 18F-FDG PET/CT led to significant management changes in 14.0% of patients (7/50). 18F-FDG PET/CT is highly effective for evaluating lymph nodes and distant metastases in PMME, and facilitates early identification of patients likely to respond to treatment. It may serve as a valuable tool for staging, response prediction, and follow-up of patients with PMME.

title: Modern Radiotherapy for Axial Giant Cell Tumor of Bone: Impact of Gross Disease at Treatment Initiation.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate outcomes of modern radiotherapy (RT) for giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB) in anatomically constrained axial sites and to assess the prognostic impact of disease burden at RT initiation. Methods We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients with pathologically confirmed GCTB of the spine, sacrum, or skull treated with RT between 2006 and 2024 at a single institution. Patients treated with palliative intent and 1 patient lost to follow-up immediately after RT were excluded. Local recurrence-free survival (LRFS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were calculated from RT initiation. Gross disease at RT was defined as a radiographically visible lesion on CT and/or MRI at RT initiation. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared by the log-rank test; prognostic factors were explored using univariate analyses. Results Seventeen patients were included (postoperative RT, n=13; salvage RT, n=3; definitive RT, n=1) and treated with 3D-conformal RT (n=9), IMRT (n=3), or proton therapy (n=5). Median follow-up was 79.8 months. The 5-year LRFS and PFS rates were 75.1% and 68.3%, respectively. Four patients experienced local recurrence and 1 developed lung metastasis. Gross disease at RT initiation (n=8) was significantly associated with inferior LRFS (5 y LRFS: 46.9% vs. 100.0% without gross disease; P=0.018). Conclusions In this cohort of axial GCTB treated with modern RT, gross disease at RT initiation was associated with inferior local control. Outcomes appeared more favorable when RT was delivered in the absence of gross disease, suggesting that maximal safe debulking before RT may be relevant in selected anatomically constrained cases.

title: What Is the Natural History and Likelihood of Progression of Indeterminate Pulmonary Nodules in Patients With Extremity Osteosarcoma?
abstract: Background Indeterminate pulmonary nodules are frequently identified on staging chest CT scans in patients with extremity osteosarcoma; however, their malignant potential and prognostic implications remain unclear. Understanding the natural history of indeterminate pulmonary nodules and the prognostic value of individual nodule characteristics is important to help guide surveillance and management decisions. Questions/purposes (1) What proportion of indeterminate pulmonary nodules progress to overt pulmonary metastasis, and what is the median time to progression? (2) Are specific radiographic characteristics-such as size, number, laterality, and calcification-associated with nodule progression or survival? (3) Do patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules at diagnosis have inferior overall survival compared with patients without pulmonary nodules? Methods We retrospectively reviewed 202 pediatric and adult patients with extremity osteosarcoma treated at a single institution between January 2016 and December 2022, with follow-up until June 2024. At initial presentation, we created three distinct study groups based on baseline high-resolution chest CT findings (0.625-mm slice thickness): group 1, those with indeterminate pulmonary nodules (patients presenting with any number of pulmonary nodules measuring < 10 mm [n = 40]); group 2, those without pulmonary nodules (patients with no detectable lung nodules [n = 146]); and group 3, those with metastasis (patients with pulmonary nodule(s) measuring ≥ 10 mm [n = 16]). Of the 40 patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules, 58% (23 of 40) were male and 43% (17 of 40) were female, with a median (range) age at presentation of 16 years (7 to 53) High-resolution CT chest images of the indeterminate pulmonary nodule group were independently reviewed by a blinded radiologist, characterizing nodules by size (≤ 5 mm versus 6 to 10 mm), number, distribution, laterality, and calcification. Longitudinal nodule behavior was classified as progressive, regressive, or static. Progression was defined as an increase in size ≥ 1 mm or in number by ≥ 1; while regression was defined as a decrease in size ≥ 1 mm or in number by ≥ 1, with remaining nodules stable. Confirmed pulmonary metastases were defined specifically as any initial baseline indeterminate pulmonary nodule that demonstrated growth to a maximum diameter of > 10 mm during the longitudinal follow-up period. Chest CT scans were done before surgery and at completion of therapy. Thereafter, chest CT scans were performed every 3 months for the first 3 years, every 6 months between years 3 and 5, and annually after the fifth year. Survival outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods, and the association of nodule characteristics with survival was assessed with Cox proportional hazards regression. Results Overall, 58% (23 of 40) of indeterminate pulmonary nodules progressed across the follow-up period, with 25% (10 of 40) of patients developing confirmed pulmonary metastasis; the median (range) time to nodule progression was 19 months (3 to 22). No individual nodule characteristic-including size, number, laterality, or calcification-was associated with progression or survival on multivariate Cox regression analysis. (1) What proportion of indeterminate pulmonary nodules progress to overt pulmonary metastasis, and what is the median time to progression? (3) Do patients with indeterminate pulmonary nodules at diagnosis have inferior overall survival compared with patients without pulmonary nodules?

We retrospectively reviewed 202 pediatric and adult patients with extremity osteosarcoma treated at a single institution between January 2016 and December 2022, with follow-up until June 2024. Progression was defined as an increase in size ≥ 1 mm or in number by ≥ 1; while regression was defined as a decrease in size ≥ 1 mm or in number by ≥ 1, with remaining nodules stable. Chest CT scans were done before surgery and at completion of therapy. Thereafter, chest CT scans were performed every 3 months for the first 3 years, every 6 months between years 3 and 5, and annually after the fifth year. title: What Is the Validity of Traction MR Arthrography for Detecting Lesions of the Ligamentous-Fossa-Foveolar Complex in Patients Undergoing Joint-preserving Surgery Through Surgical Hip Dislocation?
abstract: Background Accurate preoperative characterization of intraarticular abnormalities is important when planning hip-preserving surgery in young, active patients. Lesions of the ligamentum teres and the associated acetabular fossa and fovea capitis (forming the ligamentous-fossa-foveolar complex [LFFC]) are frequently observed intraoperatively, although their relationship with hip pain in patients without osteoarthritis remains uncertain. These lesions have received limited attention in preoperative imaging. Questions/purposes (1) What is the intraobserver and interobserver reliability of traction MR arthrography for assessing lesions of the LFFC? (2) What is the diagnostic performance of traction MR arthrography for detecting these lesions compared with intraoperative findings at surgical hip dislocation? Methods Between April 2019 and April 2022, we retrospectively identified 214 hips from a consecutive cohort of patients undergoing surgical hip dislocation at a single tertiary hip preservation center. We performed this surgery for a variety of indications, including for symptomatic femoroacetabular impingement, childhood hip diseases, and for surgically treating acetabular fractures. During this period, preoperative MR arthrography was part of the routine preoperative work-up in all patients for assessment of intraarticular abnormalities, planning for intraoperative instrument and graft needs, and prognostic purposes. MR arthrography results were not considered when choosing surgical approach. Patients without traction MR arthrography were excluded. A total of 70 patients were available for final analysis. Traction MR arthrography served as the index test and intraoperative assessment during surgical hip dislocation as the reference gold standard. The decision to perform surgical hip dislocation was based on the clinical and standard radiographic evaluation and generally not influenced by traction MR arthrography findings. Six observers (three board-certified orthopaedic surgeons with expertise in hip-preserving surgery and three board-certified radiologists with specific expertise in musculoskeletal imaging) independently conducted measurements twice using an adapted version of a previously validated grading system (grade 0, normal; grade I, degeneration; grade II, partial defect; grade III, complete defect); for diagnostic performance, findings were dichotomized as lesion absent (grade 0) or present (grade > 0). Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) with 95% confidence interval (CI) were calculated to assess intraobserver reliability and interobserver reproducibility of the adapted grading system. The diagnostic performance of traction MR arthrography for detecting lesions of the LFFC using intraoperative findings as a gold standard was determined by calculating sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, accuracy, and positive and negative likelihood ratios. Results Intraobserver reliability ICCs ranged from 0.54 to 0.69 for ligamentum teres lesions, 0.21 to 0.64 for fossa lesions, and 0.30 to 0.64 for fovea lesions. Interobserver reproducibility ranged from 0.71 to 0.84 for fossa lesions, 0.73 to 0.77 for fovea lesions, and 0.78 to 0.79 for ligamentum teres lesions. Traction MR arthrography demonstrated limited diagnostic performance for lesion detection. The sensitivity was 86% for ligamentum teres lesions, 79% for fossa lesions, and 75% for fovea lesions, whereas specificity was low at 32%, 52%, and 50%, respectively. Overall accuracy ranged from 54% to 67%. Conclusion In this cohort of patients undergoing surgical hip dislocation, contrast-enhanced traction MR arthrography demonstrated limited ability to detect and grade lesions of the LFFC preoperatively. Future prospective studies using standardized imaging protocols are needed to determine whether diagnostic performance can be improved. Level of evidence Level III, diagnostic study.

title: Histopathological Patterns in Bullous Dermatitis Artefacta: A Retrospective Case Series.
abstract: Background Dermatitis artefacta (DA) is associated with self-harming behaviors, which can be conscious or unconscious. It is characterized by lesions with atypical distributions and geometric patterns, produced by manipulation of the skin through friction, suction, heat, cold, electric current, or chemicals. Diagnosis is challenging, and there are no confirmatory tests, but histology can provide important clues for identifying artificial causes. Objective Our aim was to retrospectively review histological characteristics and anatomopathological patterns in patients with bullous DA. Methods We performed a retrospective chart review of patients with a diagnosis of bullous DA. Patients with self-induced skin diseases related to other psychic causes (such as anxiety, depression, or obsessive-compulsive disorder) were excluded. Fifteen cases were analyzed between 2009 and 2024. Biopsies were submitted to histological analyses using different techniques including hematoxylin-eosin, periodic acid-Schiff, and direct immunofluorescence, with investigation of IgA, IgM, IgG, and C3. Results Histopathology showed 4 main patterns: subepidermal blisters with neutrophils, spongiotic blisters with sparse necrotic keratinocytes, dermoepidermal or mixed cleavage blisters with follicular compromise, and "erythema-multiforme-like" blisters with extensive necrosis. Conclusions Dermatologists are uniquely positioned to diagnose and manage DA. Nevertheless, when clinical diagnosis is inconclusive, recognition of these histopathological patterns may provide valuable diagnostic clues for dermatopathologists evaluating biopsies from patients with suspected DA.

title: Neutrophilic Fixed Drug Eruption Mimicking Neutrophilic Dermatosis: Two Cases, Including Sequential Biopsies Demonstrating Time-Dependent Histopathology.
abstract: Abstract Fixed drug eruption (FDE) is classically a lymphocyte-predominant interface dermatitis, but an early lesion may show a prominent neutrophilic infiltrate that closely simulates a primary neutrophilic dermatosis. We report 2 cases. The first, a 42-year-old woman, developed a multifocal eruption approximately 45 minutes after re-exposure to etoricoxib, recurring at previously affected and new sites. A punch biopsy performed 21 hours after ingestion of the drug showed a basketweave stratum corneum, intense papillary dermal edema with pseudovesiculation, and a superficial and deep infiltrate rich in neutrophils with karyorrhexis, closely resembling Sweet syndrome. Only occasional apoptotic keratinocytes were present within the epidermis, and the marked edema obscured any interface dermatitis, although admixed eosinophils were noted. Clinicopathologic correlation ultimately established the diagnosis of neutrophilic FDE. The second, a 55-year-old man, had an eruption recurring at the same sites after pseudoephedrine. A biopsy of an established lesion 2-3 weeks after ingestion showed classic interface dermatitis with numerous eosinophils and pigment incontinence, whereas one taken from the same region within 24 hours of re-exposure showed a neutrophil-predominant infiltrate with prominent karyorrhexis and only focal interface change. These cases, biopsied at documented time points, support the concept that the neutrophil-rich appearance of FDE represents an early phase in its histopathologic evolution, demonstrate how it can be mistaken for a neutrophilic dermatosis in the absence of adequate clinical history, and show that clinicopathologic correlation and a high index of suspicion are necessary to reliably arrive at the correct diagnosis.

title: Diagnosis and Management of HIV-Associated Colitis.
abstract: A 63-year-old male with a history of untreated HIV presented to the emergency room with acute on chronic watery diarrhea, weight loss, fatigue, fever and chills. His vital signs were within normal limits and his abdomen was soft, nondistended and tender to palpation in 4 quadrants without peritonitis. He did not have leukocytosis on presentation. CD4 count was 310. CT scan showed inflammatory changes in the rectum and sigmoid colon. Comprehensive infectious workup was negative for any pathogens including cytomegalovirus (CMV), cryptosporidium, chlamydia, gonorrhea, C. difficile, cryptococcus, tuberculosis (TB) and herpes simplex virus (HSV). Colonoscopy was performed and showed a continuous area of nonbleeding ulcerated mucosa in the rectum, sigmoid, descending and transverse colon (Fig. 1). Pancolonic biopsies revealed active colitis with focal areas of basal plasmacytosis and crypt branching in left colon, suggestive of acute on chronic colitis and possible ulcerative colitis (UC). Gastroenterology and infectious disease were consulted and patient was started on IV methylprednisolone for presumed UC flare. Over the next few weeks, the patient proceeded to develop melena as well as increased lower abdominal and pelvic pain with intermittent fevers despite IV steroid treatment. The patient was trialed on IV infliximab also without significant improvement. After several weeks of steroid and biologic treatment, he developed increased abdominal pain with tachycardia and hemodynamic instability. His examination was significant for peritonitis with abdominal distension concerning for fulminant colitis. Colorectal surgery was consulted and proceeded to do an emergent total abdominal colectomy and end ileostomy. Intraoperatively he was found to have a small anterior distal rectal perforation. The decision was made to drain this area widely with rectal drain and fecal diversion and start him on IV antibiotic therapy. His final pathology from the index operation showed ulceration and acute colitis. There was no chronic crypt architectural distortion such as crypt dropout, disarray, crypt branching or basal plasmacytosis that are often seen in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). There was also increased apoptotic bodies and mitoses that were not consistent with IBD. After reviewing the clinical presentation, his disease progression, and final pathology, the treating team diagnosed the patient with HIV-associated colitis.

title: Lower-extremity Deep Vein Thrombosis after Plastic Surgery: Clinical Characteristics and Outcomes in a Retrospective Case Series.
abstract: Background Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a significant complication in plastic surgery, particularly affecting the lower extremities. Understanding the associated characteristics can aid in developing effective prevention strategies. Methods We conducted a retrospective, quality improvement-oriented case series of 5 ultrasound-confirmed symptomatic postoperative lower-extremity DVT events after plastic surgery under general anesthesia at a single institution (January 2020-May 2024). Among 39,055 general anesthesia procedures during the study period, de-identified records were reviewed for patient and procedural characteristics, prophylaxis and mobility pathways, duplex ultrasonography confirmation, management, and short-term outcomes. No non-DVT comparator cohort was extracted; analyses were descriptive and not intended for risk-factor inference. One patient with postoperative chest/back pain and transfer for suspected pulmonary embolism without in-hospital lower-extremity DVT confirmation was excluded from the final case series. Results The 5 included cases were clinically heterogeneous and involved complex perioperative settings, including post-massive weight loss body contouring, craniofacial reconstruction with implant use, neurosurgical-related reconstruction, extensive head and neck lesion surgery, and posttraumatic facial reconstruction. All DVTs were confirmed by duplex Doppler ultrasonography, with thrombi involving the posterior tibial, peroneal, or calf muscular veins. Several cases involved prolonged procedures, reoperation for postoperative hematoma, or delayed mobilization. Postoperative anticoagulation was administered in most cases, whereas postoperative mechanical prophylaxis was not consistently documented. Conclusions In a very low-frequency setting, this series highlights potentially actionable prevention gaps-especially postoperative mechanical prophylaxis and mobility disruptions-rather than establishing causal risk factors.

title: Multicenter Study on the Surgical Treatment of Suprascapular Nerve Entrapment Syndrome.
abstract: Background Suprascapular nerve entrapment syndrome is a rare but increasingly recognized cause of shoulder pain and dysfunction, particularly among young or middle-aged men involved in overhead sports or physically demanding occupations. The suprascapular nerve, primarily motor but also containing sensory fibers, may become compressed due to anatomical variations, ossified ligaments, or space-occupying lesions such as paralabral ganglia. Diagnosis is challenging due to nonspecific symptoms and overlapping pathologies and often relies on clinical evaluation supported by electromyography (EMG) and magnetic resonance imaging. Methods Between 2008 and 2018, a total of 10 patients (8 men, 2 women; mean age 31.1 y) with suprascapular nerve entrapment underwent open surgical decompression. All patients experienced chronic shoulder pain unresponsive to conservative treatment. Surgical exposure followed a scapular spine incision, allowing visualization and decompression of the nerve at the suprascapular notch and infraspinatus fossa. Follow-up (mean 15.4 mo) assessed pain (visual analog scale), muscle strength (Medical Research Council Scale), and EMG findings. Results Most patients had delayed diagnosis (mean 7 mo). At follow-up, all but 1 showed significant pain reduction during exertion (mean visual analog scale score from 4.2 to 2.7) and improved strength (mean Medical Research Council Scale score from 2.6 to 4.2). EMG demonstrated normalization in 6 patients, partial recovery in 3, and persistent myogenic changes in 1 case, possibly due to neuralgic amyotrophy. Conclusions Open surgical decompression proved to be an effective treatment for suprascapular nerve entrapment, particularly in cases unresponsive to conservative therapy or associated with secondary compression.

title: Dual-purpose Laparoscopy and Bipedicled Anterolateral Thigh Flap for Abdominal Wall Reconstruction After High-voltage Electrical Burn.
abstract: High-voltage electrical burns involving the abdominal wall pose complex management challenges, including delayed bowel perforation, progressive tissue necrosis, and durable reconstruction in compromised tissue. To our knowledge, no standardized approach has been described that combines visceral surveillance with abdominal wall reconstruction in this setting. We report a case of a 43-year-old man who sustained a 22,000-volt electrical injury with 30% total body surface area burns and a full-thickness lower abdominal wall defect (16 × 13 cm) exposing the intact peritoneum. Triple-contrast computed tomography on day 3 excluded bowel perforation. On day 22, diagnostic laparoscopy was performed for delayed visceral surveillance; in the absence of bowel pathology, intraperitoneal onlay mesh reinforcement was performed during the same procedure. On day 27, a bipedicled anterolateral thigh fasciocutaneous flap was elevated; sequential 10-minute bulldog clamp testing of each perforator produced equivalent reductions in perfusion, prompting a 4-day delay for choke-vessel maturation. On day 31, the flap was re-elevated and transposed, with the fascia lata sutured to the anterior rectus sheath as a second reinforcement layer superficial to the intraperitoneal onlay mesh. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient demonstrated complete wound healing, stable abdominal wall integrity without clinical hernia on physical examination or with Valsalva maneuver, independent ambulation with a below-knee prosthesis, and return to modified work duties. This integrated single-stage laparoscopic approach combining delayed visceral surveillance with definitive abdominal wall reinforcement may inform management of similar injuries.

Triple-contrast computed tomography on day 3 excluded bowel perforation. On day 22, diagnostic laparoscopy was performed for delayed visceral surveillance; in the absence of bowel pathology, intraperitoneal onlay mesh reinforcement was performed during the same procedure. On day 27, a bipedicled anterolateral thigh fasciocutaneous flap was elevated; sequential 10-minute bulldog clamp testing of each perforator produced equivalent reductions in perfusion, prompting a 4-day delay for choke-vessel maturation. On day 31, the flap was re-elevated and transposed, with the fascia lata sutured to the anterior rectus sheath as a second reinforcement layer superficial to the intraperitoneal onlay mesh. At the 6-month follow-up, the patient demonstrated complete wound healing, stable abdominal wall integrity without clinical hernia on physical examination or with Valsalva maneuver, independent ambulation with a below-knee prosthesis, and return to modified work duties. This integrated single-stage laparoscopic approach combining delayed visceral surveillance with definitive abdominal wall reinforcement may inform management of similar injuries.

title: From Failure to Flow: Indocyanine Green Improves Preoperative Mapping for Lymphaticovenular Anastomosis After Negative Contrast-enhanced Ultrasonography.
abstract: Accurate identification of functional lymphatic vessels is essential for lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA) but it remains challenging. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) is increasingly used for preoperative mapping; however, failure to detect vessels of adequate caliber often leads to deferral of LVA. We report a case where CEUS indicated no suitable lymphatic vessels intraoperatively, yet a high-quality LVA was successfully performed using preoperative indocyanine green (ICG) lymphography-guided exploration. Preoperative ICG mapping revealed limited linear channels and dermal backflow, guiding targeted incisions. Intraoperatively, functional lymphatic vessels and suitable venules (0.3-0.4 mm) were identified despite failed CEUS-guided localization, and end-to-end anastomosis was completed. Postoperatively, maximal interlimb circumference difference decreased from 2.5 to 1.7 cm, with symptomatic relief. This is the first case demonstrating that when CEUS-guided intraoperative localization fails, individualized ICG findings can guide empirical incisions to identify better lymphatic vessels for LVA. A multimodal approach may improve patient outcomes.

title: Pneumothorax Following Botulinum Neurotoxin Injection for Trapezius Hypertrophy.
abstract: Botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) injection into the trapezius muscle is increasingly performed for aesthetic contouring. However, iatrogenic pneumothorax has not been previously documented for this cosmetic indication, despite the inherent anatomical risks. We report a 26-year-old woman who developed immediate severe radiating pain during bilateral trapezius BoNT type A (BoNT-A) injections using a 4.8-cm, 25-gauge needle. During the injection, the patient experienced immediate severe radiating pain, followed by pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea within 30 minutes. Computed tomography confirmed a 30% left pneumothorax, effectively ruling out systemic botulism. Subsequent ultrasound revealed a skin-to-pleura distance of only 2.27 cm at the injection site, highlighting the stark mismatch with the 4.8-cm needle used. The patient was managed conservatively with high-flow oxygen, achieving complete clinical and radiographic resolution within 1 month. This case underscores that pneumothorax is a real risk with blind injection techniques and overly long needles. To minimize harm, practitioners should adhere to anatomically defined safe zones, select conservative needle lengths, and utilize ultrasound assistance when necessary, particularly for thin patients.

title: Robot-assisted Deep Inferior Epigastric Perforator Flap Breast Reconstruction: First Reported Case in the Middle East Gulf Region.
abstract: Despite encouraging early outcomes, robot-assisted deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) reconstruction has yet to be widely adopted because of its technical complexity, cost considerations, and limited institutional experience. We report the first robot-assisted DIEP flap breast reconstruction performed in the Middle East Gulf region. A 53-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer, prior irradiation, implant-based reconstruction, and severe capsular contracture underwent robot-assisted DIEP flap reconstruction using a transabdominal preperitoneal approach. Preoperative computed tomography angiography demonstrated a short intramuscular perforator course and nontortuous pedicle anatomy. Robotic pedicle harvest was completed through a 2-cm fascial incision and three 8-mm robotic ports, with a console time of 77 minutes. The flap was successfully transferred without intraoperative complications. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 3. At 5-month follow-up, there was no evidence of flap compromise, abdominal bulge, or hernia. This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of robot-assisted DIEP flap reconstruction in a carefully selected patient and highlights the successful implementation of robotic microsurgical breast reconstruction within a developing regional program. As the first reported robot-assisted DIEP flap reconstruction in the Middle East Gulf region, this report contributes to the growing but still limited global experience with robotic autologous breast reconstruction.

title: Palatal Island Flap With Adjuvant Radiotherapy for Hard Palate Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma: 2-year Outcomes.
abstract: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the minor salivary glands most commonly arises in the hard palate and exhibits perineural invasion, indolent growth, and late recurrence, often requiring multimodal therapy. Reconstruction must restore oronasal separation, speech, and deglutition; data regarding the tolerance of palatal island flaps to postoperative radiotherapy and long-term functional outcomes remain limited. A 35-year-old woman with T1N0M0 ACC of the right hard palate (American Joint Committee on Cancer, 8th edition) underwent wide local excision with partial palatal ostectomy followed by reconstruction using a contralateral palatal island flap. After complete mucosal healing, adjuvant intensity-modulated radiotherapy (66 Gy in 33 fractions) was administered. Two-year outcomes were assessed using Thai-language validated versions of the EORTC QLQ-C30, EORTC QLQ-HN43, FACT-H&N, and UW-QOL questionnaires. Final pathology demonstrated cribriform and tubular ACC with perineural invasion. The tumor approached the medial (0.4 mm) and lateral (1.7 mm) margins, which were close but uninvolved. Acute toxicity consisted of grade 2 donor-site oral mucositis treated with topical triamcinolone. At 2-year follow-up, surveillance with magnetic resonance imaging of the skull base, computed tomography of the chest, and bone scintigraphy demonstrated no evidence of locoregional recurrence or distant metastasis. Speech was fully intelligible on speech-language pathology assessment, the Functional Oral Intake Scale score was 7, and quality-of-life outcomes remained favorable across all instruments. This case suggested that a palatal island flap may tolerate adjuvant radiotherapy when irradiation is delivered after complete flap healing, with favorable oncological, functional, and quality-of-life outcomes at 2 years.

title: Biopsy of Secondary Angiosarcoma Arising in Native Mastectomy Skin of a Reconstructed Breast Without Prior Radiotherapy.
abstract: Secondary breast angiosarcoma usually develops after radiotherapy or in the setting of chronic lymphedema. We report a rare case of non-radiation-associated secondary cutaneous angiosarcoma arising in the native mastectomy skin overlying a reconstructed breast after immediate tissue expander placement and delayed deep inferior epigastric perforator flap reconstruction for breast cancer. The patient's clinical course, imaging, histopathological findings, and treatment were retrospectively reviewed. The clinicopathological features were compared with previously reported cases of angiosarcoma arising after breast reconstruction without radiotherapy before angiosarcoma onset. A 45-year-old woman underwent right mastectomy, axillary dissection, and immediate tissue expander placement for right breast cancer (T2N1M0, stage IIB), followed by delayed deep inferior epigastric perforator flap reconstruction 1 year later. No adjuvant radiotherapy was administered. Three years after the initial breast cancer surgery, progressive purpura and dark violaceous nodules developed in the native mastectomy skin. Skin biopsy confirmed cutaneous angiosarcoma. Histology showed atypical endothelial proliferation forming irregular vascular channels; tumor cells were positive for ETS-related gene and cluster of differentiation 34; the molecular immunology borstel-1 index was approximately 40%; and MYC proto-oncogene expression was observed in 60%-70% of tumor cells. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography showed no distant metastasis. Because the cutaneous disease was diffuse and surgical local control was judged difficult, multimodal treatment with pazopanib and radiotherapy (70 Gy) was initiated, followed by trastuzumab plus paclitaxel for local progression. No distant metastasis was present at the latest follow-up, although local control remained challenging. Persistent or progressive dermatitis-like lesions in postmastectomy breast skin should prompt early biopsy even in patients without prior radiotherapy.

title: Congenital Melanocytic Nevus Mimicking a Coccygeal Pad in the Sacrococcygeal Region.
abstract: Congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN) is a benign melanocytic proliferative lesion that presents at birth or in early infancy. When the lesion extends into the deep dermis or subcutaneous tissue, it can form a mass that is clinically and radiologically indistinguishable from other soft tissue tumors. We report a case of sacrococcygeal CMN mimicking a coccygeal pad. An 18-year-old man presented with a sacrococcygeal mass and tenderness. Magnetic resonance imaging and needle biopsy findings suggested a coccygeal pad. Because of persistent pain and the patient's desire for removal, the mass was excised under general anesthesia with periosteal inclusion, and the resulting 95 × 50 mm defect was reconstructed using a right superior gluteal artery perforator flap. Histopathological examination confirmed CMN without malignant features. The flap survived completely, and the postoperative course was uneventful. Tenderness resolved completely, and no local or symptomatic recurrence was observed at 6 months. CMN should be considered in the differential diagnosis of sacrococcygeal masses, and needle biopsy may be insufficient for diagnosing deeply infiltrating lesions.

title: The Hidden Trap: Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome Masking Entrapped Great Occipital Nerve-A Case of Headache Surgery.
abstract: Headache syndromes may coexist with peripheral nerve entrapment, which can obscure the true pain generator and delay effective treatment. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is a rare, painful ophthalmoplegia syndrome characterized by unilateral orbital pain and cranial nerve palsy, often showing a marked response to corticosteroids. We report the case of a 56-year-old woman with a long history of migraine who developed recurrent right-sided orbital pain, maxillary pain, and ophthalmoplegia. She was diagnosed with Tolosa-Hunt syndrome by an experienced neurologist after skull magnetic resonance imaging and clinical evaluation. Because steroids and anti-inflammatory treatment produced only partial relief, and because she also had occipital pain with a positive Tinel sign over the greater occipital nerve, occipital neuralgia was suspected. A diagnostic block of the right greater occipital nerve provided partial improvement, after which right-sided surgical decompression of the nerve was performed. At 1-year follow-up, the patient had no residual surgical sensory deficit, no recurrent severe orbital or maxillary pain, and a marked reduction in attack frequency and intensity. Her Migraine Disability Assessment score improved from 18 to 4, and medication use decreased to sporadic use of simple analgesics and triptans. In selected patients, rare headache syndromes may coexist with occult peripheral nerve entrapment. Persistent symptoms despite appropriate medical treatment should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis and targeted evaluation for occipital neuralgia.
